analysis.one_liner: Caps rent-to-own fees at state retail-installment limits and requires full price disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with small weekly payments and an option to buy. The bill would have applied the same fee caps that states put on installment credit sales to these stores, required price tags showing the cash price and the effective annual interest rate, and banned abusive collection tactics like threatening criminal prosecution. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers, who the bill's findings say are concentrated in low-income and minority neighborhoods. They would see the cash price, the number of payments, and an annual percentage rate on every item, pay fees no higher than those allowed for a comparable installment sale, and gain protections from threats and harassment during collections, with damages of $250 to $2,500 per violation plus attorney fees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a price tag on every rent-to-own item showing the cash price, the annual percentage rate, the payment amount and number of payments, and the total cost to own the item [S3].
Bars sellers from charging interest or fees higher than what state law allows on a comparable retail installment sale, and caps termination fees at 5% of the cash price [S2] [S3].
Applies the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to rent-to-own collections and prohibits threatening criminal prosecution, coercion, harassment, and deceptive claims about 'free' services [S3].
Gives customers the right to sue for actual damages plus statutory damages and attorney fees, with FTC enforcement of the rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers, whose business model has relied on charging far more over time than the item's cash price without ever disclosing an interest rate. They would face fee caps, mandatory price tags, and lawsuits for violations. Consumers in states with weak fee caps would see only modest price relief.

drawbacks.text: The fee cap is set by each state's rules for installment sales, so customers in states with weak or no caps get little protection; the bill does not set a national price limit [S2] [S3].

The bill would federalize and, in effect, legitimize the rent-to-own format as a distinct transaction type rather than reclassifying it as a credit sale, which some consumer advocates have argued leaves the underlying pricing structure in place; it also permits new termination and recovery fees up to 5% of the cash price plus reasonable recovery fees [S3].
Compliance costs — tag printing, disclosure paperwork, and lawsuit exposure — fall hardest on small independent rent-to-own stores and would likely be passed into prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the customers the industry targets, disclosure alone is a large gain: a customer renting a television might pay two to three times its cash price without ever seeing an interest rate, and this bill would have put that number on the tag. The main weakness is the fee cap's dependence on state law, which limits how much prices actually fall where states are permissive. The compliance cost to stores is real but proportionate to the harm the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on May 25, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers came out ahead. They kept a business model in which, by the bill's own findings, dealers often fail to disclose key terms and charge excessive fees and rates, with no federal requirement to show customers a cash price, a total cost to own, or an annual percentage rate. Customers kept paying undisclosed markups.

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no one else cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: These stores profit by charging weekly payments that add up to far more than the item's cash price, without disclosing a rate, and the bill's findings say they target low-income and minority neighborhoods and often charge excessive fees. Fee caps, mandatory cash-price and APR tags, and lawsuit exposure would cut directly into that revenue.

industries.industry: Collection agencies hired by rent-to-own dealers
industries.note: The bill would make the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act apply to rent-to-own collections and ban threats of criminal prosecution and harassment, restricting tactics these collectors have used.
